claims.text: A page exists at /docs/support/provider-support-policy/ (the Provider support policy page) that the Support index card links to.
The Pulumi Provider support policy page describes how long Pulumi maintains each provider major version and which providers receive long-term security updates.
Pulumi does not automatically roll back changes made during an update if an error or failure occurs; it completes pending operations in progress, then exits and reports the error.
To perform a manual rollback after a failed deployment, revert the code and configuration changes and run `pulumi up` to return infrastructure to its previous state.
Pulumi does not automatically query the cloud provider's live state before running `pulumi up` or `pulumi preview`; it compares the desired state in the program against the last recorded state.

Refreshing requires a round-trip to the cloud provider for every resource in a stack, which adds significant latency, especially for large stacks; not refreshing automatically is an intentional Pulumi design decision.
Running `pulumi refresh` synchronizes Pulumi's recorded state with the actual state of cloud resources.
`pulumi up --refresh` refreshes state and applies the desired state in a single step.
Pulumi Cloud provides built-in drift detection for automated drift detection and remediation on a schedule.
The page /docs/iac/concepts/state-and-backends/ has a 'Refreshing state' section explaining refresh behavior.

In Pulumi, the logical name of a resource is part of the auto-assigned resource URN and only needs to be unique within a stack, while the physical name is the name known to the cloud provider and typically must be unique within a certain scope (sometimes globally).
Pulumi auto-naming creates each resource's physical name by combining the logical name with a random suffix appended afterwards, e.g. `my-bucket-d7c2fa0`.
Pulumi auto-naming allows Pulumi to replace resources with less downtime by creating the replacement before deleting the old resource.
Auto-naming can be disabled on a per-resource basis in Pulumi, yielding precise physical names without random suffixes.
Project or stack configuration can be used to customize or disable auto-naming globally, per provider, or per resource type.
During a Pulumi update, secrets are decrypted in memory and visible to the Pulumi program.
Passing `--secret` to `pulumi config set` causes the value to be encrypted so it can be safely persisted in `Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml`.
For every stack, Pulumi Cloud manages a unique encryption key used to encrypt that stack's secrets, and this is configurable to use a custom secrets provider.

Because a different key is used per stack, encrypting the same value across two stacks produces different encrypted strings in the `Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml` files, so an encrypted value cannot be copied between files with a text editor and `pulumi config set` must be used instead.
When running a preview, update or destroy, Pulumi decrypts secret data, which is plain text during deployment execution and accessible by any part of the Pulumi program via the config object.
Pulumi does not use the Terraform engine in any way.
Some Pulumi providers use the open-source Terraform schemas to determine available resources and parameters and return/response attributes.
Pulumi native providers are mapped directly to cloud provider APIs and do not use Terraform schemas.
Pulumi is a declarative tool that uses imperative languages to define the end state; the language is used for authoring the program and not for talking to the cloud provider API.
Pulumi uses strongly typed languages that support IntelliSense and the Language Server Protocol, so users rarely need to leave their IDE when defining Pulumi programs.
Pulumi experimental features are always opt-in, enabled explicitly with a flag, command, or environment variable such as `PULUMI_EXPERIMENTAL=true`.
Pulumi experimental features are not necessarily supported and can change or be removed at any time without a deprecation cycle.
Pulumi's provider version support policy is to actively support the latest released major version of the providers Pulumi maintains.
For a set of widely used providers, Pulumi also ships security updates for the previous major version for up to a year, or until the next major version is released, whichever comes first.
A page at /docs/support/provider-support-policy/ (the provider support policy) exists and lists the covered providers and what a long-term support release contains.
Pulumi-maintained provider major versions older than the previous major (in the security-update window) receive no patches at all.
The Pulumi Registry lists the current version for all providers maintained by Pulumi.
Major provider versions typically include significant changes such as deprecations, new resources and new functionality, which may require additional migration steps.
Minor provider versions typically include new resources and features, performance improvements, and bug fixes without introducing breaking changes.
Pulumi recommends updating to the latest minor version on the current major at least quarterly and reviewing provider release notes.
In npm, the tilde operator (e.g. `~1.2.3`) allows patch updates on the current minor version.
Provider patch versions are primarily for bug fixes and security updates and are designed to be fully backward compatible.

Each major version of a Pulumi provider includes migration logic to smooth the upgrade from the immediately previous major version, but these migrations do not always work across multiple major versions.
Pulumi advises never being two major provider versions behind.
Pages exist at /docs/support/faq/secrets-config/, /docs/support/faq/pulumi-cloud/, and /docs/support/faq/policies/ (ESC FAQ, Pulumi Cloud FAQ, Pulumi Policies FAQ).
Pulumi actively maintains the latest released major version of every provider it publishes.
For a set of widely used providers, Pulumi ships security updates for the previous major version for up to 12 months, or until the next major version is released, whichever comes first.
The providers that receive long-term support updates on eligible older versions are AWS, Azure Classic, Azure Native, Azure AD, Command, Docker Build, GCP, Kubernetes, TLS, and Vault.
The registry link targets exist: /registry/packages/aws/, azure/, azure-native/, azuread/, command/, docker-build/, gcp/, kubernetes/, tls/, vault/.

A Pulumi provider LTS release contains High/Critical CVE security patches: fixes for CVEs affecting the provider's code or its direct dependencies, and fixes for broken internal infrastructure on the LTS branch needed to ship them.

A Pulumi provider LTS release does not contain new upstream API versions, new resources or properties, performance improvements, non-security bug fixes, or compatibility with newer language runtime versions.
Pulumi LTS providers are compatible with the version of the Pulumi engine they were frozen at, unless otherwise prompted by security fixes.
Exactly one long-term support major version exists per covered provider at any time.

When major N+1 of a covered provider ships, it becomes the new N, the old N becomes the new LTS major, and the old LTS major reaches end of life on the same day regardless of how much of its 12-month window remained.
Within the LTS major version of a covered provider, only the latest minor version receives patches; earlier minors are frozen.
Pulumi provider LTS releases are available through the same standard package registries as current-major releases, but are tagged differently.
Customers pinning to a specific major version of a Pulumi provider automatically receive patch releases as they ship, and pinning to a major version is the recommended approach.
At any time exactly one major version of a covered provider is the LTS version, and older majors receive no patches.
N is the latest released major version: if v3 is newest, v3 is N, v2 is N−1 (LTS), and v1 and earlier are end of life.
The current major (N) of a Pulumi provider receives new features, new resources, bug fixes, security patches, dependency upgrades, and new upstream API versions until N+1 ships.
The long-term support version (N−1) receives security updates in the provider's code or direct dependencies for up to 12 months from N's release, or until N+1 ships.
Provider versions N−2 and older are end of life, not supported, and will not receive updates.
The page /docs/support/faq/infrastructure/ contains a section 'What are the best practices for maintaining provider versions'.
The pages /registry/ and /docs/support/getting-support/ exist.
